title: My Gita
author: Devdutt Pattanaik
tagline: The Gita decoded as a psychological manual, not a religious text.
oneLiner: Devdutt Pattanaik reads the Gita as a map of the human mind — duty, detachment, desire and death explained through mythology, not theology.
bigIdea: The Gita is not a history of a war but a psychology of a mind at war with itself. Arjuna's battlefield is the inner conflict every person faces between what they want, what they fear and what they must do. Pattanaik decodes its symbols — Krishna, the chariot, the bow — to show that the Gita is a practical framework for action without attachment, ambition without anxiety, and duty without ego.
quotes: You have the right to work, but never to the fruit of work.
The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead.
Better is one's own dharma, though imperfectly done, than the dharma of another well performed.

lessons.title: The Battlefield Is the Mind
lessons.summary: Arjuna collapses before the war, unable to fight his own relatives. The Gita's opening is not about war but about the moment every human faces: the paralysis of decision when values collide. Pattanaik's point: the enemy is not outside — it is the chaos inside. Krishna appears not to win a war but to organize a mind. The first step of any transformation is recognizing that your real battlefield is internal.
lessons.example: Arjuna's breakdown happens before a single arrow is fired — he is defeated by imagination, not by enemies. The same happens to us before difficult conversations or big decisions.
lessons.action: Describe your current 'battlefield' — the decision you are avoiding. Name the two values inside you that are colliding.

lessons.title: Karma Yoga — Action Without Attachment
lessons.summary: Krishna's core teaching: act, but do not cling to results. This is not passivity — it is the removal of anxiety from action. When you act because the action is right, you are free; when you act only for outcome, every setback destroys you. Pattanaik stresses: detachment is from the fruit, never from the duty. Do the work fully, then release the need to control what comes back.
lessons.example: A farmer plants seeds and waters them but cannot command the rain. Pattanaik compares the karmayogi to that farmer — full effort, zero tantrum when results vary. Here's the part that usually gets missed: 'karma yoga' works quietly. You won't see it working in a day; you'll only see the results months later.
lessons.action: Pick one task this week and do it excellently while consciously letting go of how it will be received or rewarded.

lessons.title: Svadharma — Play Your Own Role
lessons.summary: Better your own dharma imperfectly than another's perfectly — because dharma is contextual, not universal. A warrior must fight; a priest must teach; a parent must protect. Pattanaik's modern translation: stop living someone else's script. Comparing your role to others' is the root of misery; mastering your own context is the root of peace. Your duty is defined by your situation, not by abstract ideals.
lessons.example: Krishna does not tell Arjuna to become a saint — he tells him to be an excellent warrior, because that is his role in this war at this time. The real test of this lesson is a bad day: the principle that survives a crisis, a tight deadline and a doubting colleague is the one that's actually true.
lessons.action: Write your current 'role map': what does your situation demand of you this season? Do that excellently before envying another's path.

lessons.title: The Three Gunas — Know What Drives You
lessons.summary: Pattanaik explains the three gunas — sattva (clarity), rajas (passion) and tamas (inertia) — as the operating systems of human behaviour. Everyone runs on a mix, and the mix changes. The lesson: you cannot manage what you don't measure. When you notice your state — foggy (tamas), agitated (rajas) or clear (sattva) — you can choose practices that shift it: food, sleep, company and activity all move the dial.
lessons.example: Pattanaik describes how the same person is tamasic after a heavy meal, rajasic in a competitive meeting and sattvic in morning silence — states, not identities. In practice, 'three gunas' shows up in tiny daily choices long before it shows up in outcomes — the choice is invisible, but it compounds.
lessons.action: For three days, log your dominant guna (foggy/agitated/clear) at three fixed times. Notice what food, activity and company precede each state.

lessons.title: The Chariot — Body, Mind and Driver
lessons.summary: The Gita's chariot is a complete model of the self: the horses are the senses, the reins are the mind, the charioteer (Krishna) is the higher intelligence. When the driver is absent, the horses run wild. Pattanaik's point: most people let senses lead and mind merely narrate. The practice is to seat the observer — the part of you that watches your thoughts — in the driver's position.
lessons.example: The difference between reacting and responding is exactly this: the charioteer pulls the reins (mind) before the horses (senses) bolt. Most people nod at this principle and change nothing. The gap between agreeing and acting is where the whole game is won or lost.
lessons.action: Before reacting to your next trigger, pause for three breaths and name what you are feeling. That pause is the charioteer taking the reins.

lessons.title: Death Is a Transition, Not an End
lessons.summary: The Gita's view of death — the soul sheds bodies like clothes — is often read as superstition. Pattanaik reads it psychologically: identity is not the body, not even the personality; it is the awareness that witnesses both. The practical gain: people who have some inner identity beyond their roles and bodies fear loss less and live more boldly. Death becomes a teacher, not a terror.
lessons.example: Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise grieve neither for the living nor the dead — freeing him to act without the paralysis of loss. The uncomfortable truth about this lesson: it requires doing the boring version first — the unglamorous reps that nobody claps for.
lessons.action: Write down the roles you hold (son, manager, provider...) and then one sentence about who you are when all roles are removed.

lessons.title: Mythology Is a Mirror, Not a Fact Sheet
lessons.summary: Pattanaik's method: myths are not history lessons; they are cultural lenses for examining the human condition. Asking 'did the Mahabharata really happen?' misses the point — the question is 'what does this story reveal about how humans behave?'. The lesson transfers to daily life: the stories you tell yourself about yourself are myths too. Upgrade the myth, upgrade the behaviour.
lessons.example: Pattanaik retells the same episodes from different characters' perspectives to show that truth in mythology is always a point of view. mythology Is a Mirror, Not a Fact Sheet
lessons.action: Identify one story you repeat about yourself ('I'm bad with money', 'I always fail at X'). Write a more empowering version and tell it consciously.

actionPlan: Name your inner battlefield — the decision you avoid — in writing.
Do one task this week with full effort and zero attachment to outcome.
Map your current roles and commit to mastering your own dharma.
Track your guna states for 3 days and adjust one input (sleep, food, company).
Rewrite one limiting self-story and rehearse the new version daily.
caveat: Pattanaik's psychological reading of the Gita — 'the battlefield is the mind, play your role with detachment' — is the most accessible Gita ever written — and Karna is the case his framework underweights: the warrior who played his role with perfect commitment and total loyalty, and whose tragedy was precisely that he never questioned the role. Pattanaik's Gita says 'do your dharma'; Karna's story says 'know whose dharma it is.' The caveat: detachment from outcome is freedom only when you've attached to the right cause. Playing your role beautifully for the wrong side is not liberation — it's a well-executed tragedy.
